Patient demographics:

  ethnicity: African

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Loss of Control: Lack of control
  Maladaptive Strategies: Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, Hopelessness: I have no future

Vignette:
Adekunle used to love the sounds of the kitchen—the sharp chop of a knife, the roar of a gas flame, the clang of a dropped pan. Now, they were just part of a landscape of noise he had to constantly sift for threats. At twenty-one, he was a sous chef in a bustling downtown restaurant, a job that once felt like the first step toward his own place. Six months ago, that future had felt certain. Now, he was certain of nothing, least of all himself. The change began on a cold night after his shift. He was walking to his car when another vehicle screeched to a halt beside him. The assault that followed was a blur of powerlessness and engine noise. Pinned against the cold metal of his own car, the overwhelming roar of their idling engine filled his head, punctuated by the brutal finality of their violence. That sound, the low, guttural rumble of a powerful engine, became a hook that could pull him back into that moment without any warning.

In the weeks that followed, the city’s soundscape became a minefield. A truck rumbling past his apartment window at night was no longer just a truck; it was them, coming back. The sound would instantly bring the memory flooding in, not as a coherent story, but as a sensory assault. He would hear the specific growl of their car’s engine in his head, as real as if it were just outside, and his body would tense for a fight he’d already lost. When he tried to explain what happened to his concerned roommate, the words wouldn't form a straight line. He would start, then find himself lost in a detail, the narrative thread slipping through his fingers until he trailed off into a frustrated silence, leaving them both feeling helpless. To cope, he learned to push the memories away, to detach and watch them from a distance as if they had happened to someone else, a character in a grim film.

His work, once his sanctuary, became a source of constant tension. The kitchen was a place of sudden movements, and he found himself flinching every time a colleague turned too quickly or reached for a tool. Each unexpected motion put him immediately on guard, a jolt of adrenaline leaving him shaky and breathless. He started constantly checking his own body, a frantic, internal scan for injury, as if the physical harm were still an active threat. Even at home, the feeling of being on guard never left him. He would lie in bed, heart pounding, cataloguing every creak of the building, every distant siren. He found a strange, grim comfort in meticulously planning his revenge, spending hours imagining turning their violence back on them. These fantasies were a dark refuge, the only place where he felt a flicker of the control he had so completely lost.

Over the months, a deep and unshakable shame took root. He was certain that somebody else—a stronger man, a smarter man—would have stopped the event from happening. He replayed it endlessly, searching for the moment he could have changed the outcome, always concluding that his failure was a moral one. He felt he had acted in ways that went against the very core of who he was; he had been weak, compliant, and that felt like a betrayal of his own values. This self-loathing curdled into a profound hopelessness. He looked at his life and saw only the wreckage. The idea of dating, of being touched, was impossible. The ambition that had once burned so brightly in him felt like a distant memory belonging to another person. He had no future; the men in the car had taken it. He finally sought help after an incident at work where a backfiring delivery truck sent him diving to the kitchen floor, convinced he was under attack. Lying there, amidst the stunned silence of his colleagues, he understood that he couldn't live like this anymore, terrified of a world where every sound was a threat and every shadow hid a monster.
